title: I.R.S. Opens Criminal Probes as Part of Trump’s Pursuit of Left-Wing Groups
summary: An internal I.R.S. memo viewed by The New York Times reveals how the agency is carrying out President Trump’s orders to investigate “domestic terrorism.”

The Internal Revenue Service has initiated at least four criminal investigations as part of the Trump administration’s crackdown on left-wing groups that began after the killing of Charlie Kirk last year, according to an internal agency memorandum viewed by The New York Times.


The pages of the memo viewed by The Times do not identify the subjects of the investigations, nor is their current status known. But even the existence of the criminal investigations is the clearest sign yet that President Trump has successfully dragged the typically technocratic I.R.S. into enforcing his political agenda.


The memo describes the work done by a group of a dozen I.R.S. officials detailed to a task force formed in response to Mr. Kirk’s death on Sept. 10, 2025. Mr. Trump[ordered agencies](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/09/countering-domestic-terrorism-and-organized-political-violence/) across the government to investigate the antifascist movement, or antifa, and other groups that espouse “extremism on migration, race and gender,” among other views.


Under that order, the I.R.S. was told to investigate whether nonprofits were “directly or indirectly financing political violence or domestic terrorism.” In March, officials from the criminal investigations branch of the service began working with the task force out of the F.B.I. headquarters.


The I.R.S. work on the task force has also involved rapid response to events like protests at Delaney Hall, an immigrant detention center in Newark, N.J., the memo states. Protesters and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have[repeatedly clashed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/nyregion/delaney-hall-protests-photos.html?eafs_enabled=false) at the site, and a Democratic member of Congress is among the people who have[been charged with a crime](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/26/nyregion/lamonica-mciver-newark-assault-charges.html?eafs_enabled=false) after an encounter with federal agents there.


I.R.S. officials reviewed financial information, including subpoenaed Venmo records, about people arrested during those protests, as well as businesses that the officials believed could be funding them. At one point, I.R.S. officials used facial recognition and tattoo analysis databases to help identify individuals, the memo said.
